newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Family of dead IRA suspect call for private funeral.
newsitem.headline: Family of dead IRA suspect call for private funeral.

text.p: The family of an Irish man shot dead in a police raid on a London IRA bomb factory said on Tuesday they did not want his funeral to be turned into a guerrillas' farewell.

Eoghan and Theresa O'Neill said in a statement to the media that they wanted the funeral of their 21-year-old son Diarmuid to be a private affair and urged reporters to stay away from this small community on southern Ireland's West coast.

"Although we would prefer a private funeral, we nevertheless welcome all men and women (as private individuals) of goodwill who might wish to join us in our prayers," they said in a statement issued in Britain and Ireland.
"The occasion is one in which our thoughts are entirely private. We would like Diarmuid's funeral to reflect our love for him and sorrow at his death," the statement said.

It was apparently aimed at Irish Republican sympathisers to prevent O'Neill's funeral being turned into a traditional IRA sendoff with a volley of shots over a tricolour-draped coffin by men in paramilitary uniform.
The statement said reporters and television crews, many of whom have been scouring the Timoleague area for days for background stories on the family, would not be welcome.

O'Neill was gunned down last week, apparently unarmed, when police raided a London house and found tonnes of explosive, automatic weapons and other equipement they said was to have been used by an Irish Republican Army (IRA) cell.

His death has provoked allegations from Irish Republican sympathisers in Britain and elsehwere that police were operating a "shoot-to-kill" policy against the IRA, which has fought British rule of Northern Ireland for 25 years.
O'Neill's parents complained at the weekend that their son had not been given a fair trial and said they would never know whether or not he was involved with the IRA.

Four men arrested in the raid were remanded in custody in London on Tuesday on charges of possessing arms and explosives which police said were for use against strategic targets in London in a new campaign to wring concessions from Britain.
O'Neill was born of Irish parents but was brought up in Britain. His parents bought a holiday home in this scenic village overlooking the sea in which they plan to spend their retirement.
He is expected to be buried in the Roman Catholic church which dominates Timoleague on Thursday afternoon after his body has been flown back from a mortuary in London, residents said.
They said the body would not be given the traditional "removal" ceremony from the local undertakers but would be taken direct to the church and buried at a brief ceremony.

The funeral coincides with a crisis in Anglo-Irish attempts to negotiate a political settlement for Northern Ireland because of continued IRA violence and warnings that the IRA's Protestant Loyalist foes may break a self-imposed truce.
